Headline: Recording the Century: Media Formats, 1877–2006
Text: How did people capture, store and share sound, images and information? This timeline follows the formats that shaped the 20th century, from wax cylinders to MP3s, along with a few 19th-century precursors and one 21st-century epilogue. Use the group labels (Sound, Moving image, Broadcast, Photography, Digital & data) to follow a single thread, or the filter buttons above to show one at a time.

Headline: Phonograph cylinder
Text:
Thomas Edison's 1877 tinfoil phonograph was the first machine that could both record and play back sound. Wax cylinders, sold commercially from about 1889, became the first mass-market recorded-music medium; Edison kept making them until 1929.

Why it matters: Sound became something you could own, carry home and replay.

Learn more: Phonograph cylinder (Wikipedia)
Media Credit: M. Dupres / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0
Media Caption: A phonograph cylinder.
Alt Text: A brown wax phonograph cylinder standing upright.

Headline: The Horse in Motion
Text:
Eadweard Muybridge photographed a galloping horse with a row of cameras, showing a sequence of still frames that could be played back as motion. This chronophotography is a precursor to film, not yet film itself.

Why it matters: It showed that a series of still images could record movement.

Learn more: The Horse in Motion (Wikipedia)
Media Credit: Eadweard Muybridge, public domain
Media Caption: Muybridge's 1878 photographs, animated.
Alt Text: Animated black-and-white sequence of a jockey riding a galloping horse.

Headline: Motion picture film: Roundhay Garden Scene
Text:
Louis Le Prince shot the oldest surviving motion picture, about two seconds long, in Leeds in October 1888. Film then went from short silent "actualities" shown in nickelodeons to synchronized-sound features, Technicolor, and classroom filmstrips.

Why it matters: Moving images could be captured on a single strip and projected to audiences.

Learn more: Roundhay Garden Scene (Wikipedia)
Media Credit: Louis Le Prince, public domain
Media Caption: A frame from Roundhay Garden Scene (1888), the oldest surviving film.
Alt Text: Grainy frame showing four people walking in a garden.

Headline: Gramophone disc
Text:
Emil Berliner's flat disc records, sold in the United States from the mid-1890s, were easier to mass-produce than cylinders. Shellac discs spinning at about 78 rpm became the standard record format until the 1950s.

Why it matters: Flat discs could be stamped by the thousands, which helped create the record industry.

Learn more: Phonograph record (Wikipedia)
Media Credit: Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
Media Caption: An early Berliner Gramophone disc.
Alt Text: A single-sided early gramophone disc with an engraved center label.

Headline: Kodak Brownie camera
Text:
Kodak's Brownie sold for one dollar and used roll film that Kodak developed for the customer. It made snapshot photography affordable for ordinary families and children.

Why it matters: Photography went from a professional craft to an everyday habit.

Learn more: Brownie (camera) (Wikipedia)
Media Credit: cogdogblog / Wikimedia Commons, CC0
Media Caption: A Kodak Brownie box camera.
Alt Text: A small black box camera with a round lens on the front.

Headline: Commercial radio broadcasting
Text:
Pittsburgh station KDKA broadcast the Harding–Cox presidential election returns on November 2, 1920, often cited as the start of commercial radio in the US. KDKA grew out of engineer Frank Conrad's amateur station 8XK.

Why it matters: One transmitter could now reach millions of homes at the same moment.

Learn more: KDKA (AM) (Wikipedia)
Media Credit: T. R. Kennedy Jr., public domain
Media Caption: Frank Conrad's station 8XK, the forerunner of KDKA, in 1920.
Alt Text: Black-and-white photo of early radio transmitting equipment on a table.

Headline: Synchronized sound film ("talkies")
Text:
Warner Bros.' The Jazz Singer premiered on October 6, 1927. It used the Vitaphone sound-on-disc system for its songs and a few lines of spoken dialogue, and within a few years most new Hollywood films had sound.

Why it matters: Sound changed how films were written, acted, and exhibited.

Learn more: The Jazz Singer (Wikipedia)
Media Credit: Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
Media Caption: Theatrical poster for The Jazz Singer (1927).
Alt Text: Vintage movie poster advertising The Jazz Singer.

Headline: Three-strip Technicolor
Text:
Technicolor's three-strip camera recorded red, green and blue on separate negatives. Disney's short Flowers and Trees (1932) was the first film released in the process, and it went on to define the look of Hollywood color films.

Why it matters: Color became a normal part of feature filmmaking.

Learn more: Technicolor (Wikipedia)
Media Credit: Marcin Wichary / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0
Media Caption: A three-strip Technicolor camera.
Alt Text: A large, boxy film camera on display in a museum.

Headline: Magnetic tape recording
Text:
AEG's Magnetophon tape recorder was shown at the 1935 Berlin Radio Show. After World War II, reel-to-reel tape spread through American radio and recording studios because tape could be edited, spliced and re-recorded.

Why it matters: Editing and multitrack recording made the modern studio possible.

Learn more: Magnetophon (Wikipedia)
Media Credit: touhotus / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0
Media Caption: A later reel-to-reel tape recorder (Revox B77, c. 1977).
Alt Text: A reel-to-reel tape recorder with two large tape spools.

Headline: Electronic television
Text:
After experiments by John Logie Baird (1926) and Philo Farnsworth (1927), RCA and NBC began regular US television broadcasts at the 1939 New York World's Fair. Television spread into most American homes in the 1950s.

Why it matters: Television became the dominant mass medium of the second half of the century.

Learn more: History of television (Wikipedia)
Media Credit: Wmpearl / Wikimedia Commons, CC0
Media Caption: An RCA Victor TRK-12 television set from 1939.
Alt Text: A tall wooden cabinet television with a mirror lid that reflects the screen.

Headline: Cable television
Text:
Cable television began in 1948 in the United States as Community Antenna Television (CATV). It started independently in mountainous rural areas of Pennsylvania and Oregon, where a shared hilltop antenna fed TV signals by cable to homes that could not get clear reception.

Why it matters: Cable later made room for dozens of specialized channels.

Learn more: Cable television (Wikipedia)
Media Credit: UnifiedFunctionality / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0
Media Caption: A sign warning about a buried CATV cable.
Alt Text: A roadside sign warning of a buried television cable.

Headline: LP record
Text:
Columbia Records presented the 33⅓ rpm long-playing (LP) microgroove record at New York's Waldorf-Astoria Hotel in June 1948 (most sources give June 21; some say June 18). Made of vinyl rather than shellac, a 12-inch LP held about 20–25 minutes per side, compared with about 4 minutes for a 78.

Why it matters: The LP made the album, not the single song, the main unit of recorded music.

Learn more: LP record (Wikipedia)
Media Credit: Evan-Amos / Wikimedia Commons, public domain
Media Caption: A 12-inch vinyl LP record.
Alt Text: A black 12-inch vinyl record seen at an angle.

Headline: Polaroid instant camera
Text:
Edwin Land's Polaroid Land Camera Model 95 went on sale in Boston in November 1948. It produced a finished print inside the camera within about a minute, with no darkroom needed.

Why it matters: Instant photos made picture-taking immediate and private.

Learn more: Polaroid Land camera (Wikipedia)
Media Credit: Daderot / Wikimedia Commons, CC0
Media Caption: Polaroid Land Camera Model 95, MIT Museum.
Alt Text: A folding instant camera with a bellows, in a museum case.

Headline: 45 rpm single
Text:
RCA Victor answered Columbia's LP with the 7-inch 45 rpm record in 1949. The "war of the speeds" ended with both formats surviving: LPs for albums, 45s for singles, jukeboxes, and Top 40 radio.

Why it matters: The 45 became closely tied to rock 'n' roll and teenage record buyers.

Learn more: Single (music) (Wikipedia)
Media Credit: lynx305 / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0
Media Caption: A 45 rpm adapter, used to play large-hole singles on standard turntables.
Alt Text: A small plastic disc adapter for playing 45 rpm records.

Headline: Videotape
Text:
Ampex demonstrated the first practical videotape recorder, the VRX-1000, in April 1956. Networks could now record live television and replay it, for example in other time zones, instead of using film kinescopes.

Why it matters: Television could be recorded, edited and rerun.

Learn more: Videotape (Wikipedia)
Media Credit: Austinmurphy / Wikimedia Commons, public domain
Media Caption: Assorted videotape formats.
Alt Text: A pile of videotape cassettes of different sizes.

Headline: Cassette tape
Text:
Philips introduced the Compact Cassette at the Berlin Radio Show in August 1963. (The original timeline dated it to 1962, when it was being developed.) It is an analog magnetic tape format in a small plastic shell, and because Philips licensed it free of charge it became the worldwide standard for portable and home recording.

Why it matters: Blank tapes let ordinary listeners record, copy and make mixtapes.

Learn more: Cassette tape (Wikipedia)
Media Credit: Thegreenj / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0
Media Caption: A Compact Cassette.
Alt Text: A clear plastic audio cassette with two visible tape reels.

Headline: 8-track cartridge
Text:
Developed by a consortium led by Bill Lear, the 8-track tape cartridge was offered in Ford cars in 1965. It was an endless-loop cartridge that was popular in cars in the late 1960s and 1970s and was later replaced by the cassette.

Why it matters: It brought chosen music, rather than only radio, into the car.

Learn more: 8-track cartridge (Wikipedia)
Media Credit: Isis / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0
Media Caption: Inside an 8-track cartridge.
Alt Text: An open 8-track cartridge showing its single reel of looped tape.

Headline: Floppy disk
Text:
IBM shipped the first 8-inch floppy disk in 1971. Later 5¼-inch and 3½-inch versions became the standard way to carry software and documents between personal computers through the 1980s and 1990s.

Why it matters: Digital files became something people could hand to each other.

Learn more: Floppy disk (Wikipedia)
Media Credit: Vassia Atanassova (Spiritia) / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0
Media Caption: An 8-inch floppy disk.
Alt Text: A large square 8-inch floppy disk in its paper sleeve.

Headline: Home video: Betamax vs. VHS
Text:
Sony launched Betamax in 1975 and JVC launched VHS in Japan in September 1976. VHS offered longer recording time, won the "format war" and made it normal to time-shift TV and rent movies at home.

Why it matters: Viewers, not broadcasters, began to control when they watched.

Learn more: Videotape format war (Wikipedia)
Media Credit: LoMit / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0
Media Caption: A VHS videocassette.
Alt Text: A black VHS videocassette seen from the front.

Headline: LaserDisc
Text:
LaserDisc (first sold as DiscoVision) went on sale in Atlanta in December 1978. It was the first optical disc format for consumers, storing analog video read by a laser. It had higher picture quality than VHS but stayed a niche product.

Why it matters: Its optical technology led to the CD and the DVD.

Learn more: LaserDisc (Wikipedia)
Media Credit: Windell Oskay / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0
Media Caption: A LaserDisc, which is the same size as an LP.
Alt Text: A large silver optical disc reflecting rainbow colors.

Headline: Sony Walkman
Text:
Sony's TPS-L2 Walkman went on sale in Japan on July 1, 1979. It was a pocket cassette player with lightweight headphones, and it made portable private listening part of everyday life. Cassettes outsold LPs by the mid-1980s.

Why it matters: Music became a personal soundtrack carried through public space.

Learn more: Walkman (Wikipedia)
Media Credit: Anna Gerdén / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0
Media Caption: The original Sony Walkman TPS-L2 (1979).
Alt Text: A blue and silver portable cassette player with headphones.

Headline: Compact disc (CD)
Text:
Developed jointly by Philips and Sony, the CD went on sale in Japan on October 1, 1982, together with Sony's CDP-101 player. Billy Joel's 52nd Street was the first catalogue number. Audio is stored as digital data in microscopic pits that a laser reads. The standard disc held 74 minutes, later extended to 80. (The original timeline said 82 minutes and said the laser was used to "encode" discs; commercial CDs are stamped, and the laser reads them.)

Why it matters: The CD brought digital audio into homes and outsold cassettes by the early 1990s.

Learn more: Compact disc (Wikipedia)
Media Credit: liamz2r / Wikimedia Commons, public domain
Media Caption: A compact disc.
Alt Text: A shiny silver compact disc reflecting rainbow colors.

Headline: MP3
Text:
MP3 (formally MPEG-1 Audio Layer III) is a lossy compression format developed largely at Germany's Fraunhofer Institute. It was approved as part of the MPEG-1 standard in 1991, published in 1993, and given the .mp3 name in 1995. It removes sounds most listeners cannot hear, making files about one-tenth the size of CD audio.

Why it matters: Music could now be shared over the internet, both legally and illegally.

Learn more: MP3 (Wikipedia)
Media Credit: rfdigitalwpg / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0
Media Caption: The Diamond Rio PMP300 (1998), one of the first portable MP3 players.
Alt Text: A small dark handheld MP3 player with a monochrome screen.

Headline: MiniDisc
Text:
Sony introduced MiniDisc in 1992. It was a small recordable magneto-optical disc in a protective cartridge, combining the convenience of a cassette with digital audio. It was popular in Japan but was overtaken by MP3 players elsewhere.

Why it matters: It shows that "better" formats do not always win.

Learn more: MiniDisc (Wikipedia)
Media Credit: Ramon Vasconcellos / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.5
Media Caption: A TDK MiniDisc next to an AA battery for scale.
Alt Text: A small square MiniDisc cartridge beside an AA battery.

Headline: DVD
Text:
DVD players went on sale in Japan in November 1996 and in the US in 1997. A disc the size of a CD held a full-length digital film with menus, extras and multiple languages, and DVD became the fastest-adopted consumer electronics format of its time.

Why it matters: Home video moved from analog tape to digital disc.

Learn more: DVD (Wikipedia)
Media Credit: Wanted, Ochro / Wikimedia Commons, public domain
Media Caption: The data side of a DVD-R.
Alt Text: The purple-tinted data side of a recordable DVD.

Headline: Napster and file sharing
Text:
Shawn Fanning's Napster launched in June 1999 and let millions of users swap MP3 files peer-to-peer. After lawsuits from Metallica and the record industry, it shut down in 2001, and the industry eventually moved toward legal downloads and streaming.

Why it matters: It separated music from physical formats entirely.

Learn more: Napster (Wikipedia)
Media Credit: Steve Jurvetson / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0
Media Caption: The Napster logo laser-etched on a laptop.
Alt Text: The Napster cat-headphones logo etched onto a laptop lid.

Headline: Epilogue: cloud storage
Text:
The original timeline dated cloud storage to 1960. Its ideas go back to 1960s time-sharing computers, but commercial cloud storage arrived with services such as Amazon S3 (March 2006). In this model, files are kept on remote servers run by a provider rather than on a disc or tape the owner holds.

Why it matters: Here the 20th century's story of owning media objects ends with renting access to remote servers.

Learn more: Cloud storage (Wikipedia)
Media Credit: Carl Lender / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0
Media Caption: Server racks in a data center.
Alt Text: Rows of computer server racks with blinking lights.
